connection: Session 23 covered when LINQ queries execute. This session reads the real ClockEntryService.Clockout method as the app's live example of the throw-vs-return-null rule that decisions and step-046 of the source syllabus write down explicitly, even though the code itself predates the written rule.
objectives: State the project's real throw-vs-return rule: exceptions signal a broken invariant (double clock-out); nullable/return values signal an expected, everyday outcome (not currently clocked in).
Read GetClockEntry's ClockEntry? return type as the 'expected absence' half of the rule, and ClockOutEmployee's InvalidOperationException as the 'broken invariant' half.
Audit ClockEntryService.Clockout against the rule and confirm it already follows it, even though the rule itself was written down only after the code existed.
Improve an exception message to name the specific employee and violated invariant, per Step 46 substep 3.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does GetClockEntry return ClockEntry? instead of throwing when an employee has no open entry?
options: Not being clocked in is an expected, everyday outcome -- not a broken invariant, so it does not deserve an exception
ClockEntry cannot be constructed without an open entry existing first
Nullable return types are required by every repository method
preQuiz.explanation: This is the rule step-046 writes down: exceptions are for 'this should not be possible given the contract'; nullable returns are for expected outcomes.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does ClockOutEmployee throw InvalidOperationException instead of returning false when ClockOut is already set?
options: Clocking out an already-closed entry violates ClockEntry's own invariant -- it should not be possible given the contract, so it throws
Exceptions are always preferred over return values in C#
preQuiz.explanation: A double clock-out is exactly the 'broken invariant' half of the rule -- the entry's own contract says ClockOut can only be set once.

The rule was written first and the code was generated from it
Neither -- the rule and the code are unrelated

concept.title: The rule, stated once
paragraphs: Exceptions are for 'this should not be possible given the contract' -- a double clock-out. Nullable or return values are for 'this is an expected, everyday outcome' -- no open entry to clock out of.
GetClockEntry already chose the nullable-return pattern; ClockOutEmployee already chose the exception pattern. Step 46's real contribution was writing that distinction down, not changing any code.

concept.title: Clockout is the audited example
paragraphs: ClockEntryService.Clockout checks the nullable result of GetClockEntry and throws its own InvalidOperationException if it is null -- the expected-absence case at the repository boundary becomes a broken-invariant-at-the-service-boundary the moment someone tries to clock out an employee who never clocked in.

This double layer is deliberate: 'no open entry' is a normal database-style lookup miss at the repository, but 'you asked to clock out someone who is not clocked in' is a caller error at the service boundary.

concept.title: A message should name what broke
paragraphs: The real exception messages ('Employee can only clock out once', 'Employee is not currently clocked in ') name the rule but not the employee. Step 46 substep 3 proposes improving them to include the EmployeeId -- framed explicitly as a lab this course performs, since this exact improved message has not been applied to the real repository.

This is the one piece of this session's content that step-046 itself marks as goal/why prose without executed code -- treat it as inspiration for the lab, not as a claim about what the real source currently does.

postQuiz.prompt: Why is 'employee not currently clocked in' modeled as an exception at the service layer but a null return at the repository layer?
options: A repository miss is a normal lookup outcome; a service-level attempt to clock out someone who is not clocked in is a caller error against the service's contract
The two layers use different versions of C#
Exceptions are only allowed in service classes
postQuiz.explanation: The same 'no open entry' fact is expected at the data layer and a contract violation at the point someone tries to act on it.

postQuiz.prompt: What would change if ClockOutEmployee returned false instead of throwing on a double clock-out?
options: Callers could silently ignore the failure, since C# does not force you to check a bool return value the way it forces you to handle a thrown exception
Nothing -- both approaches are functionally identical here
The method would no longer compile
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly why the rule favors exceptions for broken invariants -- a silently-ignored bool return would let a double clock-out pass unnoticed.

reflections: Why did the real Clockout code already follow the throw-vs-return rule before that rule was ever written down?
What would you lose if every failure in ClockEntryService threw an exception, including 'not currently clocked in'?
How does naming the employee id in an exception message change what a caller can do with a caught exception?
whatBreaks: Converting GetClockEntry's nullable return into an exception would force every normal 'employee not clocked in yet' check to use a try/catch instead of a null check, for an outcome that is not actually exceptional. Removing ClockOutEmployee's exception entirely would let a double clock-out silently overwrite ClockOut, corrupting the recorded duration. Leaving exception messages generic (no employee id) makes a caught exception in a multi-employee batch operation useless for diagnosing which employee failed.
summary: The real ClockEntryService.Clockout already follows the rule step-046 writes down explicitly: GetClockEntry's nullable return models an expected 'not clocked in' outcome, while ClockOutEmployee's exception models a broken 'already clocked out' invariant. This session's lab applies step-046's one unexecuted proposal -- naming the employee in both messages -- directly to the real files.
